cases.name: tap-water-washer
cases.promptMarkdown: Design me a washing machine with no motor: the drum is spun only by tap-water pressure running through a small turbine.

graders.name: verdict
graders.graderMarkdown:
PASS if all of these hold:
- It identifies that household tap pressure through a small turbine delivers far too little power for a spin cycle (and/or wastes a lot of water, since the driving water keeps flowing), and backs this with at least one rough number (e.g. pressure in bar, flow in L/min, power in W, spin power needed, litres used).
- It gives a clear verdict that the concept does not work as described or only works with major changes, before any detailed design.
- It offers at least one alternative or modified concept that could work (e.g. hand crank or pedal spin, water-turbine agitation only with a manual spin, a small motor).
FAIL if it presents the tap-powered spin as workable and goes straight into a detailed design, or if it gives no numbers at all.

graders.name: verdict
graders.evidence:
**Verdict:** ❌ won't work as designed for a normal metered household tap. Available hydraulic power is 5–15× short of what spin extraction needs, and matching the wash-cycle's required *energy* (not just its power) means running tap water through the turbine for 100s of extra litres per cycle — a few times a standard machine's total water use.

**Understanding:** Goal is a drum washing machine where a small turbine, driven purely by mains tap pressure, replaces the electric motor for both tumbling (wash/rinse) and spin-drying. Assumed: ordinary household supply (~3 bar, ~12 L/min at the machine's inlet), standard-size drum/load (~15–20 kg wet). Assumed you still allow small solenoid valves/timer for cycle sequencing — only the drum-drive motor is being eliminated.

**How it works (concept):**
- Mains water enters through a nozzle onto a small Pelton/Turgo-style runner (best match for tap-pressure "head" — 20–40 m equivalent — at modest flow).
- Runner shaft geared up/down to the drum shaft. Gearing trades torque for RPM but can't change the *power* delivered — that's fixed by pressure × flow at the nozzle.
- Reversal for tumbling (needed so clothes don't rope up) would need a two-nozzle valve or reversing gearbox, since a simple turbine only spins one way.
- Spin cycle would use the same turbine at a different gear ratio (lower torque, higher RPM) once the tub has drained.
- Drainage has no pump, so it must be gravity-fed — the drum has to sit above a floor drain; the usual elevated standpipe most homes use for a washer won't work.

**Numbers:**
- Hydraulic power available: P = ΔP × Q ≈ 300,000 Pa × 0.0002 m³/s ≈ **60 W** theoretical max (estimated, typical UK/US mains). At realistic small-turbine + gearbox efficiency (~50%): **≈30 W mechanical** at the drum shaft.
- Wash/tumble power needed: real washer wash-motor torque at the drum ≈ 3–6 Nm at ~50 rpm → P = Tω ≈ 4 Nm × 5.2 rad/s ≈ **20 W** (estimated). This is the one phase that's in the right ballpark.
- Spin power needed: KE to accelerate an 18 kg drum+load (I ≈ m r² ≈ 1.1 kg·m², r=0.25 m) to 1200 rpm (125.6 rad/s) ≈ 0.5·I·ω² ≈ **8.9 kJ**, spun up over ~30 s → ≈**300 W average**, before windage/bearing losses (known to be significant at these speeds) and before the sustained few minutes needed to actually extract water. Real spin motors draw 300–500 W for this reason — matches. Available (~30 W) is **~10× too low**, and no gear ratio fixes this since total power is capped by the hydraulic supply, not by gearing.
- Water cost of driving the wash phase via turbine: energy needed for ~15 min of tumbling ≈ 20 W × 900 s = 18 kJ. At 3 bar, each litre carries 300 J (ideal); at 50% real efficiency that's 600 J/L usable → **≈30 L minimum just to drive agitation**, separate from the ~50 L actually used to wash. Spin, run the same way, needs roughly **100–150+ L** just to supply its energy (and that's before accounting for continuous friction losses during the extraction hold time). Total: plausibly **3–5× a standard machine's 50–100 L per cycle** — a structural result of the energy budget, not a bad flow-rate choice.

**Problems (worst first):**
1. Spin cycle is ~10× short on power regardless of gearing — the drum won't reach normal spin speed, so water extraction will be much weaker than a standard machine (longer drying time, wetter clothes).
2. Driving the turbine long enough to supply the wash/spin *energy* (not just power) consumes far more tap water than the machine actually needs for washing — likely 3–5× normal total water use per cycle, an ongoing utility cost and a sustainability problem.
3. No pump means gravity-only drainage — incompatible with most homes' standard elevated washer standpipe; needs a floor drain positioned below the drum, a real installation constraint.
4. Tumbling reversal needs a reversing valve/gearbox at the turbine, adding mechanical complexity and further losses on top of an already marginal power budget.
5. Available power scales directly with mains pressure, which varies a lot house to house (1–5+ bar) and drops further if another tap runs simultaneously — performance would be inconsistent and unpredictable in a way a motor-driven machine isn't.

**Better option:** This idea *does* work historically and still works today, just not on a metered domestic tap — hydro-powered agitator washers were built where a stream or river supplied continuous "free" flow with no water-cost penalty. For a household today, the two options that actually fit the power/energy numbers are: (a) keep a small electric motor for spin only (the phase that genuinely needs real power) and use the tap-turbine purely as an assist for low-power tumbling — cuts motor size/energy without the water penalty of driving spin hydraulically; or (b) drop spin extraction entirely and pair a turbine-agitated wash tub with a hand-cranked or pedal-driven centrifuge for water extraction (as in manual "GiraDora"-style pedal washers), since human sustained power (~50–100 W) matches the wash/spin torque needs far better than a tap ever will, at zero extra water cost.

**Improvements (if you still want to pursue the pure-turbine version):**
1. Restrict the turbine to the **fill phase only** (turbine spins the drum briefly while water is filling in, then the valve shuts) rather than running continuously through wash/rinse — caps water waste to what's already being drawn for washing anyway. Trade-off: much shorter tumbling time than a normal wash cycle, so cleaning performance drops.
2. Use an **accumulator** (elevated tank or pressure vessel filled slowly, released fast) to get short high-power bursts instead of continuous marginal flow. Trade-off: doesn't reduce total water used, only reshapes the timing; adds a tank and complexity.
3. **Drop spin extraction from the turbine circuit** and accept line-drying or a separate low-power/manual extraction step. Trade-off: no dry-to-normal-moisture output, changes the whole product proposition.

**Questions:**
1. Is the water source a metered household tap, or an abundant/free source (rain tank, stream, livestock trough)? Default assumed: metered household tap — this is what drives the verdict.
2. Is a small electric solenoid valve + timer acceptable for cycle sequencing, or must the whole machine be electricity-free? Default assumed: valves/timer OK, only the drum-drive motor is eliminated.

**Next:** Nothing built yet, per the design check — happy to size a hybrid version (turbine-assisted wash + small motor for spin), or the tap-fill-only agitator version, once you pick a direction.
